sect1.title: System Maintenance and Backup
sect1.para: A properly configured mail server is only the beginning. To ensure long-term reliable operation, regular maintenance tasks must be performed and proper backup strategies must be in place. This section covers the essential ongoing maintenance tasks required to keep your mail server running smoothly.

sect2.title: Log Rotation and Management
sect2.para: Mail servers generate substantial amounts of log data. Without proper log rotation, these files will eventually fill your disk space. OpenSuSE uses the logrotate utility to manage log files automatically.

By default, OpenSuSE configures logrotate to handle mail logs, but it's important to verify and potentially adjust these settings based on your mail volume. The configuration file is located at /etc/logrotate.d/syslog.
A typical mail log rotation configuration looks like this:
sect2.programlisting: /var/log/mail.info /var/log/mail.warn /var/log/mail.err { compress dateext maxage 365 rotate 99 missingok notifempty size +4096k create 644 root root postrotate /usr/bin/systemctl reload syslog.service endscript }
sect2.para: This configuration will:

listitem.para: Compress old log files to save disk space
Keep logs for up to 365 days
Rotate logs when they exceed 4MB in size
Reload syslog after rotation to ensure proper logging continues

sect2.title: Disk Space Monitoring
sect2.para: Mail storage can grow rapidly, especially if users don't regularly clean their mailboxes. It's critical to monitor disk space and take action before it's exhausted.
The primary areas to monitor are:

listitem.para: /home - Where user maildir folders are stored (typically in /home/username/Maildir/)
/var/spool/postfix - The mail queue, which can fill up if messages can't be delivered
/var/log - Log files, especially mail.info, mail.warn, and mail.err

sect2.title: Mail Queue Management
sect2.para: The Postfix mail queue holds messages that are waiting to be delivered. Under normal circumstances, the queue should be nearly empty. A growing queue indicates delivery problems that need attention.

listitem.para: Temporary network problems preventing connection to remote mail servers
Incorrect DNS configuration or unresolvable domain names
Remote servers refusing connections (greylisting, blacklisting, rate limiting)
Malformed recipient addresses

sect2.title: Mail Storage Backup
sect2.para: Your mail storage (the maildir folders) contains all user emails and is the most critical data to back up. A proper backup strategy ensures you can recover from hardware failures, accidental deletions, or other disasters.

sect3.title: Backup Strategies
sect3.para: There are several approaches to backing up maildir folders:

listitem.para: Full backups - Copy the entire maildir structure. Simple but can be time and space intensive.
Incremental backups - Only copy files that have changed since the last backup. More efficient but requires backup software to manage.
Rsync-based backups - Use rsync to efficiently copy only changed files to a remote location.
Snapshot-based backups - Use filesystem snapshots (LVM, ZFS, Btrfs) to create point-in-time copies.

sect3.title: Using Rsync for Maildir Backup
sect3.para: The rsync tool is particularly well-suited for backing up maildir folders because it can efficiently handle many small files and only transfers changes.
sect3.programlisting:
#!/bin/bash # Backup all user maildirs to remote server
BACKUP_HOST="backup.example.com" BACKUP_USER="backup" BACKUP_PATH="/backup/mail" SOURCE="/home/*/Maildir"
# Perform backup rsync -avz --delete \ --exclude="**/tmp/" \ --exclude="**/dovecot.index.cache" \ $SOURCE $BACKUP_USER@$BACKUP_HOST:$BACKUP_PATH/
# Check exit status if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "Backup completed successfully at $(date)" | \ mail -s "Mail Backup Success" root@localhost else echo "Backup FAILED at $(date)" | \ mail -s "Mail Backup FAILURE" root@localhost fi

listitem.para: -a - Archive mode (preserves permissions, timestamps, etc.)
-v - Verbose output
-z - Compress data during transfer
--delete - Remove files from backup that no longer exist in source
--exclude - Skip temporary and cache files that don't need backing up

sect3.para: Schedule this script to run daily via cron:
sect3.screen: $> sudo crontab -e # Add this line for 2 AM daily backup: 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup-mail.sh

sect3.title: Testing Backup Restoration
sect3.para: A backup is only useful if you can restore from it. Regularly test your backup restoration process:

listitem.para: Create a test user account
Send some test emails to the account
Perform a backup
Delete the user's Maildir folder
Restore from backup
Verify all emails are accessible via IMAP

sect3.para: Document your restoration procedure so it can be followed during an actual emergency.

sect2.title: Certificate Renewal
sect2.para: The self-signed certificates created in this tutorial have an expiration date (typically one year). Before they expire, you must generate new certificates and update the configuration.
To check when your certificates expire:
Set a reminder to renew certificates at least two weeks before expiration. Follow the same procedures described in to create new certificates, then restart the affected services:
sect2.screen: $> sudo systemctl restart dovecot $> sudo systemctl restart postfix $> sudo systemctl restart apache2

note.para: If you later decide to use certificates from a trusted CA (such as Let's Encrypt), you'll need to set up automatic renewal since those certificates expire every 90 days. Let's Encrypt provides tools like certbot that handle automatic renewal.

sect2.title: Security Updates
sect2.para: Keeping your mail server software up to date is critical for security. OpenSuSE provides regular security updates through its package management system.
To check for available updates:
sect2.screen: $> sudo zypper refresh $> sudo zypper list-updates
sect2.para: To install all security updates:
For a mail server, pay particular attention to updates for:

listitem.para: Postfix
Dovecot
Apache and PHP
OpenSSL
MySQL

sect2.para: Configure automatic security update notifications:
sect2.screen: $> sudo zypper install yast2-online-update-configuration $> sudo yast2 online_update
sect2.para: While automatic updates can be convenient, for production mail servers it's often better to manually review and apply updates during scheduled maintenance windows to avoid unexpected downtime.

sect2.title: Monitoring and Alerting
sect2.para: Proactive monitoring helps you identify and resolve issues before they become serious problems. Consider monitoring:

listitem.para: Service status (are Postfix, Dovecot, Apache running?)
Disk space usage
Mail queue size
Failed login attempts (potential attacks)
Certificate expiration dates
System load and memory usage
